profilePeriod: Premiership 1983–1991, interpreted alongside explicitly identified later public positions through 2017.
scopeNote: Answers are editorial simulations of documented political principles, not a questionnaire completed by the person. Brazil-specific statements are interpreted in the analogous home-country context. Modern hypothetical technologies require inference.

sources.title: Bob Hawke — National Museum of Australia
sources.evidence: Four election wins; consensus with employers and unions; financial deregulation; national educational standards; political memoirs published in 1994.

sources.title: Robert Hawke: during office — National Archives of Australia
sources.evidence: Created Australian Electoral Commission; Medicare; Accord; tariff and banking liberalisation; federal environmental intervention; Sex Discrimination Act 1984; Indigenous treaty proposal and ATSIC; supported UN action against Iraq.

sources.title: Towards a closer partnership — Hawke speech
sources.evidence: Proposed Commonwealth/state/local cooperation, national standards and economic management, while allowing state delivery and less tied funding; explicitly supported parliamentary democracy, individual freedom and rule of law.

sources.title: National Agenda for a Multicultural Australia — Hawke speech
sources.evidence: Defended cultural diversity and equal access, within shared Australian allegiance and institutions; English language recognition accompanied cultural and language rights.

sources.title: Brian White interview — Hawke
sources.evidence: Called himself agnostic rather than atheist, acknowledged lifelong influence of Christian principles, and denied a return to religious belief.

sources.title: Gun control agreement — Hawke media statement
sources.evidence: Announced Commonwealth/state gun-control cooperation, import restrictions on automatic and semi-automatic rifles, and measures limiting access by violence-prone people.

sources.title: Midday Show interview — Hawke
sources.evidence: Explicitly opposed capital punishment and supported efforts to prevent the execution of Australian drug offenders in Malaysia while respecting judicial guilt findings.

sources.title: Willesee interview — Hawke
sources.evidence: Defended proposed Australia Card against privacy objections as a tax-compliance measure. This supports administrative enforcement, not unlimited surveillance.

sources.title: Illicit drugs report chapter 4 — Australian Parliament
sources.evidence: Records harm minimisation in national drug strategy documents from early Hawke government in 1985; does not establish support for blanket drug legalisation.

sources.title: Radio 8DN talkback interview with Col Krohn — Hawke
sources.evidence: Defended individual choice in abortion and MPs’ conscience votes, while rejecting wholly unlimited freedom in the area.

sources.title: Brisbane press conference — Hawke
sources.evidence: Rejected claims that proposed rights protection simply entailed compulsory changes to marriage and abortion; his response is not evidence of a marriage-equality policy in office.

sources.title: Statement to Parliament on science and technology — Hawke
sources.evidence: Praised medical/reproductive research, computing and industrial innovation; created PM Science Council and Chief Scientist; insisted innovation serve human and environmental needs.

sources.title: CEDA speech — Hawke
sources.evidence: Defended tariff cuts including vehicle/textile sectors, competitiveness, retraining and business tax reductions; rejected a wage free-for-all and continued coordinated reform.

sources.title: Change is not Optional — Hawke, John Curtin Memorial Lecture
sources.evidence: Defended partial Commonwealth Bank float and fiscal discipline, while maintaining Labor social objectives and cooperative union bargaining.

sources.title: Perth press conference — Hawke
sources.evidence: Opposed ideological hostility to public ownership and ruled out privatising Telecom or Australia Post under his government; supports selective rather than universal privatisation.

sources.title: Gulf War & Iraq War — Australian War Memorial
sources.evidence: Australia joined the US-led multinational Gulf response after Iraq invaded Kuwait, with naval forces enforcing UN sanctions and participating in the 1991 war.

sources.title: Bob Hawke pushes nuclear power at Woodford — ABC eyewitness report
sources.evidence: Later public position: advocated nuclear power against global warming, paid international waste storage with proceeds aiding Indigenous people, and abolition of state governments.

sources.title: Hawke and Howard in new accord — ABC
sources.evidence: Later public position: supported same-sex marriage, contrasting with Howard at a joint Lifeline fundraising appearance.

sources.title: Hawke criticises marriage postal survey — ABC
sources.evidence: Later public position: supported marriage equality and condemned the cost and damage of the postal survey; preferred parliamentary action.

sources.title: Better Off Dead episode 17 transcript — Bob Hawke interview
sources.evidence: Hawke explicitly supported legal assisted dying for irremediable suffering, judging forced suffering unjustifiable; a later public position, not an in-office policy.

sources.title: The Hawke memoirs — Supreme Court Library Queensland catalogue
sources.evidence: Lists Robert James Lee Hawke as author, Heinemann Australia 1994, and Australian politics/government subjects.

facts: 1990 cooperative federalism sought common standards, national economic coordination and improved state service delivery.
1983 Franklin intervention overrode state development policy.
2016 publicly advocated abolishing state governments; later centralising view is explicitly included, not backdated.
estrutura.tension: National uniformity and eventual state abolition coexist with local delivery and Indigenous autonomy; do not infer dictatorship.

facts: Won four elections; electoral reform established the AEC in 1984.
1990 expressly affirmed parliamentary democracy and rule of law.
2017 opposed a marriage postal survey in favour of parliamentary responsibility.
representacao.tension: Representative democracy and institutional safeguards, rather than assemblies, sortition or plebiscitary rule.

facts: 1987 gun restrictions and 1985 Australia Card show real willingness to regulate and enforce.
1986 explicitly opposed executions; 1985 drug policy included harm minimisation.
2016 supported assisted dying.
poder.tension: Administrative security and public health alongside civil liberties; neither punitive authoritarianism nor blanket personal deregulation.

facts: 1989 Agenda celebrated diverse cultures and equality while keeping common Australian citizenship and English.
imigracao.tension: Multicultural nationalism is not unlimited migration or abolition of national identity.

facts: 1990–1991 UN-sanctioned Gulf deployment demonstrates willingness to use armed force with allies.
National Archives records active peace diplomacy in the Middle East.
diplomacia.tension: Armed collective security and negotiation, not pacifism or war for prestige.

facts: Joined US-led coalition and UN sanctions against Iraq after invasion of Kuwait.
Used diplomacy to raise Australian international standing.
intervencao.tension: International engagement and allies reject permanent neutrality, but do not support domination of neighbours or unilateral conquest.

facts: Medicare and social wage remained core.
1991 supported partial bank sale; 1990 defended public Telecom/Post.
economia.tension: Mixed ownership, welfare and unions coexist with private enterprise and selective asset sales.

facts: 1983 floating dollar and financial deregulation.
Accord coordinated wages; 1991 rejected wage free-for-all.
Fiscal discipline and business tax relief accompanied welfare priorities.
controle.tension: Strong labour coordination does not imply comprehensive price/currency controls or total planning.

facts: 1991 argued tariffs impoverished consumers and hindered exports; reduced vehicle/textile protection with transition assistance.
comercio.tension: Trade opening with adjustment support, not autarky or an immediate unregulated world market.

facts: 1990 explicitly agnostic, retaining Christian moral influence.
1989 recognised citizens across religions within common institutions.
religiao.tension: Secular law and personal ethical inheritance; neither theocracy nor eradication of religion.

facts: 1984 sex-discrimination legislation and affirmative action advanced women’s equality.
1984 abortion choice with conscience-vote protection.
2012 and 2017 supported marriage equality.
moral.tension: Equal civic rights do not automatically establish agreement with every contemporary cultural practice.

facts: 1989 funded science, industrial and medical innovation while highlighting environmental control.
1983 Franklin protection constrained development.
2016 advocated nuclear climate solutions and waste storage.
tecnologia.tension: Technological optimism coexists with protection of sensitive ecosystems and ethical limits; no transhumanist platform verified.

uncertainties: Scope: premiership 1983–1991 interpreted alongside explicitly identified later public positions through 2017, as confirmed by coordinator. Later nuclear/marriage/assisted-dying/state-abolition views are not in-office achievements.
Questions about AI, facial recognition, Bitcoin, embryo enhancement, neutral language and Brazilian institutions require transparent analogous judgements, not claimed direct statements.

Specific positions on universal adoption equality, polyamory, cultivated meat and neural implants were not established; answers are restrained inferences from civil equality, science and safeguards. N is reserved for genuine competing principles, not missing evidence.
No Brazilian translation of The Hawke Memoirs was verified by title/Portuguese searches; original title retained.
Primary transcript OCR contains errors. Dates follow transcript metadata where present; the 1991 Curtin lecture year is verified, exact day not used.
